utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Before we bring the witness in, the Trial Chamber will hand out several oral decisions, in the following order: First order. The Trial Chamber is asking the Prosecution to file, at the latest on the 1st of June, 2010, all motions which it feels it needs to file before the 98 bis decision is rendered, which means, Mr. Marcussen and Ms. Biersay, that you have until the 1st of June to file all your requests. After that, it will be too late. When once these motions have been filed, Mr. Seselj will have enough time to reply to these motions when they have been translated in his language. That is the first oral decision. The second oral decision concerns the motion filed by the OTP on 29th of March, 2010. I shall read it out slowly. Considering the motion recorded by the Registrar on the 29th of March, 2010, with a view to obtaining, in its second motion, i.e., Bar table, the possibility to exceed 3.000 words and to extend this to 4.353 words. Considering the Practice Direction in the length of motions and applications, given that the Bar table motion aims at admitting 180 documents which most relate to the speeches of the accused and the interviews he gave in the period covered by the indictment. Considering that the Trial Chamber holds that the important number -- in light of a great number of documents and the need for the Prosecution to justify each document in detail, the reasons for filing a motion, substantiate exceeding the word limit in the Practice Direction of the 16th of September, 2010. Considering that it is in the interests of justice for the accused to benefit from the same time delay if he wishes to reply to the Bar table motion. For the foregoing, we will grant the motion and order that the second Bar table motion of the Prosecution not exceed 4.400 words and, second, that the reply filed by the accused to the second Bar table motion, in the event that he would like to reply, not exceed 4.400 words. Mr. Seselj, I would like to indicate today that the Prosecutor has sent us a voluminous motion which contains seven volumes. I personally spent five hours looking into all the documents to realise that we have here three series of documents, one first series which has to do with all the interviews you had, the second series which relate to all your speeches before the National Assembly of your country, and the third series of documents are miscellaneous documents, including press articles. The first two series, i.e., your interviews and your speeches before the National Assembly, are documents which lie at the heart of the joint criminal enterprise and documents which may include incriminating evidence, i.e., to incite to commit crimes. It would be most advisable for me and my colleagues if you were to respond to these submissions to give us your opinion on each of the documents that relate to your interviews. I was about to say this is at the core of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution's motion needs to be translated for you, of course, and we have set the word limit at 4.400 words for your reply. You have 15 days to reply, but in light of the fact that this motion is exceedingly important, you could perhaps ask for additional time to respond. You may decide also not to respond. That is for you to judge. In addition, I would like to indicate that the Prosecution has filed a judicial notice on the basis of the Krajisnik judgement. There are 10 facts or so for which the Prosecution has requested a judicial notice. We also need to know your position on this. Let me, from memory, remind you that this has to do with item 24 of the Prosecution's motion. You have been mentioned specifically in the Krajisnik judgement. That said, contrary to what I had told you a few weeks ago, since I knew nothing about the motions filed by the Prosecution which have been coming in of late at an increasing pace, we will undoubtedly not be able, before the end of August or the beginning of September, start on the 98 bis procedure. In light of all the work that needs to be undertaken by the Trial Chamber for it to be able to hand down its decision relating to the two motions, and given your submissions and motions, we have every reason to believe that we will only be able to start after having completed all of this beforehand, start on the 98 bis procedure at the end of September and not, as I stipulated previously, in June, because at the time I knew nothing about the fact that the Prosecution was going to file such motions. I also have a decision that I would like to hand down in closed session. You have raised your hand. If what you have to say is very short, I will give you the floor straight away. We must not forget that a witness is waiting and our time is very valuable, because the Trial Chamber will have two hours to question the witness, the Prosecution will have two hours, and you will also have two hours, Mr. Seselj. Please make it short. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I would like to state my position about what you just said briefly, and then I have four administrative issues to raise, but that will also be brief. You can relax. I will not do what would suit you most, because I don't want to give you coverage for prejudicing my right to due process. What the Prosecution is asking for is not based in either continental or common law. I am strictly opposed to a document being admitted without a witness, but that has been done. But to allow the Prosecution to send documents by mail, that is not grounded in any kind of law. In many cases here, the accused did not have proper Defence. We had a decision concerning video-recordings. You ordered the Prosecution to bring all the video-clips, to see them in the courtroom, and the Prosecution had, according to your order, to state their arguments, and I would be given the right to respond. In the same way, the Prosecution can present their documents through witnesses one by one, explain why they're relevant, and I should have a chance to respond concerning relevance. That would be clear-cut, like with video-recordings. Now, for the Prosecution to give you a batch of documents and that I should be asked to respond, that is out of the question. The Prosecution should also make available video-recordings of my Assembly speeches, my newspaper and radio interviews, et cetera. But newspaper articles which reflect a journalist's subjective interpretation of events, for them to be admitted into evidence without any witness to corroborate it, without any chance to discuss it in the courtroom, that is absolutely out of the question. That is a dirty trick that the Prosecution is trying to make you approve, and I won't participate in it. You would be contributing to further irregularity of this process, and this process has long been completely irregular for many, many reasons. Rest assured that you can -- that you are going to save time, because I'm not going to waste it. As for judicial notice of facts determined in the Krajisnik case, gentlemen Judges, Krajisnik himself complained that he did not have adequate Defence. Do you know what happened to Krajisnik once in the courtroom? He had a witness that was cross-examined, and Mr. Krajisnik asked to ask a few questions himself. And his lead counsel got to his feet immediately and told the Trial Chamber that he is opposed to his client asking questions. That counsel kept his own client in the status of idiot in the courtroom. Mr. Krajisnik withdrew his power of attorney from that counsel, decided to defend himself in the appeals proceedings, and then engaged a new lawyer as assistant. His trial was irregular. He had inadequate Defence. What the Trial Chamber found in his case, I don't care. I do not recognise a single sentence from that judgement. A very new book will soon appear by me, "The Hague Anti-Serbian Guillotine," in which I expose the many irregularities and prejudices to the accuseds' right to due process in many cases in this Tribunal, including those in my own trial. Now, I have to raise a few administrative issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. The Trial Chamber has noted your comments. The four items you have mentioned will take up how much of your time? I'm concerned about the witness. This will be one of the last witnesses before the presentation of your case, so I would like to finish this witness. How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not revise my own evidence in this trial, but I'll try to be concise. I can't tell you straight away whether it's going to be five or ten minutes, but in the meantime, if you hadn't asked me this question, I would have dealt with one problem by now. I'll be brief. I got a letter from Soraya Laucci to Mr. Ram Doraiswamy, the Registrar of our Trial Chamber, where she says that the Trial Chamber believes that only official transcripts can be admitted into evidence and that the Prosecution should review all the transcripts admitted into evidence in the Seselj trial and up-loaded into e-court, and replace all the versions of transcripts marked "Unofficial" with the official revised version. This was a surprise to me, that revised transcripts from earlier trials were not admitted and up-loaded. And as for 98 bis evidence, I need all the submissions of the Prosecution and all decisions of the Trial Chamber which form part of the evidence. Of course, it was disclosed to me as 65 ter, but it's a huge amount of material mixed up with a lot of useless material that I have never used. Now I need it all organised in binders in the Serbian language, because I have no assistants here who can do that for me. And I believe that someone must do it for me, be it the Registry or some service of the Office of the Prosecutor. But, in any case, I need it to prepare a proper 98 bis motion. Second. In the month of April, I was visited by my legal assistants and the case manager. In fact, only the legal adviser, Boris Alexic, and case manager, Marina Ragus. The Registrar again prevented Zoran Krasic, my legal adviser, to visit me, and wrote to me that his visit could not be privileged but would instead be supervised, and that's why Mr. Krasic did not arrive. They also failed to pay the arrival -- the visit of my legal advisers, and I had to pay for all that alone. The last time they visited was in April, and God knows when they're going to come back, because I can't afford their travel. Third. On the 19th of April, I received a Prosecution motion to recall one witness. Since this is confidential material, I will not quote anything from that material. But the point is that after the witness completed his testimony, the Prosecution interviewed him again, and the witness gave them a new statement through which the Prosecution tried to rehabilitate themselves, having made a mess of it in the courtroom, because I demolished their witness in cross-examination and proved that the Prosecution is using inappropriate methods in interviewing witnesses and preparing 92 ter statements. Now they want to recall this witness. I assert that it's impossible, because if you set such a precedent, then that means that the Prosecution would be able to recall all their witnesses with all their new statements, because so far I have demolished all their witnesses. Not a single witness of theirs remains standing here in the courtroom as relevant. I have demolished all their theories and all their case. Now, if you allow them, it would mean that the Prosecution could recall all the witnesses, prepare new statements using the results of my cross-examination, and rehabilitate these witnesses in the courtroom. No, that can't be done, and that's why I oppose this motion. The fourth issue. Several months ago, you gave me your verbal decision that I have to preventively submit to you for censure -- censorship all the material that I want to have published. I haven't done that yet, but my books are appearing in publication, and most recently my book -- my police dossier has appeared. This is my police file from the beginning of 1982 through the end of 2002, 20 years of police work to collect the information about me, through informers, through wire-tapping, through placing bugs in my apartment, et cetera. This contains a large amount of documents that the Prosecution obtained from the Government of Serbia. I asked the Government of Serbia to give me those documents as well, but the Government of Serbia told me that I must not show it to anyone, that I can't publish it, that I must ask for their consent to use it in the courtroom, et cetera, et cetera; but how can the Government of Serbia bind me to such an undertaking? I'm prepared to be arrested one day by the Government of Serbia. It's their business. I don't care. Now, after they gave all this to the Prosecution, I asked them to give me the rest of my police file from the years which are not relevant to the indictment. So in a moment of weakness, they provided me with that as well, possibly to sooth their conscience after delivering so many Serbs to The Hague Tribunal, and I decided to publish it in its entirety. What can they do about it? I'm sitting in prison in The Hague, so I can't be sitting in the prison in Belgrade at the same time. But the Prosecution can relax from now on. Whenever they give me any new documents, they don't have to bother to mark it "Contact the Serbian government before use in court." That's now irrelevant. I've published it all in the Serbian language in the original. Gentlemen Judges, as far as I know, it has never happened yet anywhere in the world that a political opponent of the regime has published his entire police file. I am the first, and I'm proud of it. Now, when you look at these four books, when you see all the things that the secret police, led by Jovica Stanisic, did against me, you will understand how pointless it is for the Prosecution to place me in a joint criminal enterprise with Jovica Simatovic and -- Jovica Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic when I was an opponent of the regime. And even when I was a member of the government of Serbia, the secret police wire-tapped me as a terrorist who is just looking for his first chance to overthrow the government by force. That's why this is important. And it's important for another reason. I had understood your inclination to accept police files and police material as evidence. In Serbia, that's impossible. It's still impossible. Only when the witness -- or, rather, the accused or a suspect is interviewed in the presence of his lawyer, then such material is admissible. However, reports from informants cannot be admitted into evidence. You have been inclined to accept such material. Now, if you look how many horrible lies have been planted against me in the past 20 years, and when you grasp all the methods that the secret police had been using in Yugoslavia, when you see that for the past 20 years I have been on the edge between life and death, you will understand then that you cannot trust a single police report. Therefore, be kind and order the Legal Officer to take these books and give them to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I shall give the floor to Mr. Marcussen, who was on his feet. What would you want to do with your books? Would you like them to be admitted? Would you like to give them to the Trial Chamber? What status should these books have, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before Mr. Marcussen takes the floor, I did not want the books to be admitted. I'm just respecting your decision, and that decision has not been delivered to me in writing. I'm just informing you that the books are out of print and I am giving them to you for your inspection, and you do whatever you want to do with them. You can keep them as a souvenir, you can sell them. They will sell well. They're expensive. You can give them to somebody as a gift. I hope that you will not throw them away. I'm not giving a set to the Prosecution because they can buy themselves a set in Belgrade. Maybe they will charge me with the contempt of court for this, but they can go to Belgrade and buy themselves a set of my books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was on my feet because the accused was not raising an administrative matter, but promoting one of his books and making substantive submissions. The other thing is obviously there is no reason for the accused to give the book to the Trial Chamber for inspection, because your order was that it should be given before publication. This book has been published, so whatever is in the book is out there already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, the Chamber has handed down a decision. I do not have the reference, but this can be found. We said that in future, when the accused would publish a new book, this book would have to be submitted to the Registry in order to check whether there are not anything in the book that could cause prejudice to the peaceful unfolding of the hearing, the reputation of the Tribunal, or that of the Judges. It seems that those books do not meet those criteria. But I find a potential interest for yourself, but this is your problem, really. If, in this book, you state that you were under surveillance from policemen from Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, and this happened over a number of years, this could be interesting when dealing with the joint criminal enterprise, because you are in a joint criminal enterprise with those other two persons, as well as others. And perhaps in those police reports could perhaps state that you had a talk with Mr. Karadzic or with Mr. Milosevic or that you were put under wire-tapping. I don't know. Unfortunately, I do not read your language, and therefore it would be very difficult for me to look into what is being said and to understand what's in the book. But I will ask my colleagues what we are going to decide regarding those four books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber deliberated on those issues, and they are asking the usher to go and fetch those books, to give them to the Registrar, and according to our decision, the Registry, with their translators, will look at the content of those books and will draft a report, if necessary; namely, if the book is of any interest to us. So this is our decision. Mr. Usher, could you go and fetch those four books and give them to the Registrar, who is in this room. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just to be sure that we understand the order, what is being checked is whether or not there is any material that shouldn't have been disclosed; the Chamber is not minded to look at the books as evidence, since it has been tendered? It's just a formulation of what Your Honours said. It's to check whether or not there is disclosure of confidential information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Two very brief comments, and then we will bring the witness into the courtroom. But I have to also read another oral decision, which is rather long. So first my remarks. A witness had been then heard by the Prosecutor. I was rather surprised when I saw that. I could not, in the least, imagine that a Prosecutor would have a talk with a witness, so I was rather surprised, and I hope that this will not happen again. Secondly, regarding the talk with Mr. Krasic, we heard that there was no interview with Mr. Krasic because you had learned that he was going to be wire-tapped during this interview. And being aware of this, you say that under those conditions, there is no point for him to come over here. We were aware of this, because we had been informed by the Registry. As for the other questions that you raised, they are of a technical nature and we will handle those issues between each other. I would like to ask the Registrar to move to closed session. I have a rather long oral decision to read, and then we will bring the witness into the courtroom. Please, let's move to closed session, because we are dealing with a protected witness in this oral decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please confirm that you are not asking for any protection measures and that you are prepared to testify in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you give us your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zoran Rankic. I was born on the 1st of August, 1955, in Bogatic, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I work as a foreman in a construction company. I'm a construction technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, have you already testified before a court of law on events which unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is that the first time that you testify in a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. You may sit down. Witness, some information regarding the way this hearing will unfold. In the first stage, you will answer to questions put by the three Judges before you. We have decided to split those two hours into three, so each and every Judge will have about 40 minutes. Personally, I'm not going to use the full 40 minutes, given the delay that we've encountered this afternoon. After that, the Prosecutor will have two hours. The Prosecutor made a motion to change the rounds; namely, that they wanted for Mr. Seselj to first ask questions and then the Prosecution, but the Chamber has not accepted this request, given that we have always proceeded the same way; Judges questions, judges [as interpreted] from the Prosecution, and questions from the accused. But given the Prosecutor has two hours, they can use 90 minutes for the questions first, and then they can give the floor to Mr. Seselj, who can use two hours, and then they can take the floor again for another 30 minutes. This being said, the Prosecution will have, all in all, two hours, not one more minute and not one minute less. If they do not use their two hours, it's all the better, but they have two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection. I don't accept your method. This is something new, you've just introduced something totally new. In that case, I'm not going to examine the witness. If you give half an hour to the Prosecutor after my examination, I won't examine the witness. You can give the Prosecution four hours if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, in that case, if you give this up, it is your choice. But, Mr. Seselj, the Chamber gives you the opportunity to take the floor again after additional questions from the Prosecutor. So the Prosecutor may have 90 minutes, then you use 90 minutes, and then the Prosecutor uses 30 minutes for additional questions, and then you take the floor last and then you have another 30 minutes. So perhaps you did not understand what we had decided upon. You can always take the floor last. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood you well the first time 'round. Maybe the interpretation was not good. Now that you've corrected yourself, or maybe the interpreter did not interpret correctly the first time 'round, now I understand that I have the last word and I always have the last word after the Prosecutor. Maybe it was not interpreted properly the first time 'round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we all agree. Witness, I'm going to start putting questions to you. I devoted several hours in looking at documents, such as statements made to the Prosecutor. The Prosecution, as well, has questions to put, Mr. Seselj, and then this allows me to look at the entirety of the picture. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you perhaps tell us under which circumstances you first made statements with the Prosecution, and then in August 2008 you went to see the Defence team of Mr. Seselj to give them a statement? Could you perhaps tell us why you were, in the first stage, a Prosecution witness and then you were a Defence witness for Mr. Seselj? Could you please give us some explanation regarding this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I have to start with the year 2003. That's when my first statement was given to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. And I have to finish with the year 2006, and that was the time when I provided my last statement to the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, and that was here in The Hague. From 2003, the OTP started putting pressure on my family. They wanted me to report to the Office of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade because they wanted to take my statement. I hope that I'm not talking too fast. Am I? And since they were putting a lot of pressure on my family for me to report to them, and they threatened me that if I did not report to the OTP, I would be brought in by the organs of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, in order to protect my family from ill treatment I responded to their invitation. The first time, they questioned me for three days. It was Mr. Paolo Pastore Stocchi who was the investigator in charge, and there was also Ms. Sabine Scholz who was there. I started providing my statement according to the best of my recollection. You know the events had happened a long time ago, and it was only logical that I couldn't remember some of the events. Mr. Paolo Pastore Stocchi was not satisfied with the statement that I provided. He tore up the first statement that I provided, and he said, Mr. Rankic, either you're going to give us a proper statement, and you have to know that we have statements by other witnesses which do not tally with what you're telling us. I suppose that he thought that my statement was false, that I was not telling the truth, that I was lying, and the course of the interview evolved in the following way: Mr. Rankic, I know that you are not a sweet-smelling flower. We have something for you. We have statements by other witnesses to the effect that you were present during some events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And my conclusion from all of that was that if I did not co-operate with him, I could suffer consequences, all of that could have repercussions on my life from then on. At that time, I was not sure whether the OTP of The Hague Tribunal could bring charges against me for something that I really was not a part of. I personally did not feel guilty. I don't feel guilty. I personally know that I did not participate in any war crimes. I know that I never tried to cover up a war crime either. I was perplexed, I was afraid. At that time, my family situation was very bad. As a result of all that, I divorced my wife. I did not live with my family. I was unemployed at the time. I started drinking as well. My health was not good at the time, and it's still not good. I have a lot of health problems. I started giving statements. The first one was given -- as far as I remember, the interview lasted for three days, and the interpreter read my statement back to from her laptop. And on the end of day 3, I was given a bunch of papers to sign. Can you imagine what my state was after the three days of interrogation? I could hardly wait to sign all that, to sign the statement, and to leave the Office of The Hague Tribunal. I just wanted to go in and have some rest. I wanted to give my brain some rest from all of that. It is very difficult to try and remember things that happened 15 or 20 years ago and still be as concentrated as you possibly can be. My second encounter with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal was at the beginning of 2004. The investigators were a woman, whose name was Rita, and I believe she was from Nepal - I can't remember her family name - and there was a gentleman from Sweden whose name I believe was Thomas Athans [phoen]. Ms. Rita from Nepal threatened me and told me that if I did not -- if I did not co-operate with the investigators, I could be delivered to Bosnia, because allegedly in Bosnia they had something against me, they could put me on trial for something, although I know that I knew then that that wasn't true. At such a moment, nobody would be indifferent. I know that heaps of Serbs have been sentenced here to long-term imprisonment, so I was forced to start giving untruthful statements in order to save my hide. And it then ended, and then in 2006 I was again invited to the Office of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade. I had a conversation there with Mr. Daniel Sax [as interpreted], who was a Prosecutor at the time, and he told me on that occasion that all of my cases had gone missing at the airport in Belgrade and that there is an imminent danger that I would be assassinated; that it would be good if I came to The Hague to give all my statements again and to supplement some of the things that I had said before. I wasn't very clear on the origin of that imminent danger because of that -- because of that -- before that I was not endangered by anybody, and especially not by the Serbian Radical Party, where I still have friends today. I had them at that time, I still have them, although I'm not a member of the Serb Radical Party. I haven't been a member since 1993. I just want to say that nobody ever threatened me or nobody ever intimidated me. I arrived here in the Hague with an explanation that I would spend a few days here. However, that dragged on and lasted nearly two months. In the meantime, Mr. Seselj's trial was about to start. He was dissatisfied with some of our decisions, he went on a hunger strike, and that's why the beginning of trial was postponed. They probably planned for me to be the first Prosecution witness, since I was already in The Hague. Since all that did not materialise, and I realised that nothing would come out of that, later on they tried to promise me that I would be relocated to a third country, that I would be financially provided for, to be safe. I don't know who should I have been safe from, because nobody ever threatened me. I am not easily scared, I am not easily intimidated by anybody. I was deceived, and I left The Hague. Actually, I was the one who tricked them, and I left The Hague. I could no longer sit here. They didn't send me to any third country, as they had promised they would. I returned to Belgrade. And a few days later, although I was not in my house, the Serb police was looking for me at my -- at the address where my residence is, but I don't reside there. After that, I didn't know what to do. I called the Serbian Radical Party, and a gentleman by the name of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to interrupt you here. You have described to us everything that happened with the OTP. I shall get back to a point of detail a little later. Now, please explain to me how things happened with Mr. Seselj's Defence. Did members of Seselj's Defence team contact you or did you contact them? Can you give us some details, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I understood your question, and I have just started to explain all that. I called the Serbian Radical Party, and the gentleman replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you saying is important. You are testifying under oath. Each and every word is important. When you say, I am the person who phoned up the Serbian Radical Party, you know that, through technical means, we are able to know whether you did, in effect, call or not the Serbian Radical Party. We can check whether you phoned that number, and we professional Judges can check all that out. I hope you have understood me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I say, with full responsibility, and I know that I'm here to testify under oath, I respect this Tribunal, I consider this Chamber a professional Chamber. That's why I'm here to tell the truth and the whole truth. I was the one who called the Serbian Radical Party, and a gentleman replied. His name was Dragan Tasic. I told them that I could no longer be in touch with the OTP, that I didn't want to be in touch with them. And I said that if the Trial Chamber summoned me, I would respond to those summons, but I would never respond to the summons of the OTP. And then he told me to draft a statement and to send it to them. I drafted a statement. I personally drafted a statement. Nobody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me on what date this was, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting the question to you because I have a statement that is dated the 12th of August, 2008. Did you make a statement prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I got mixed up on the year. My first statement, as far as I can remember, was provided in 2007, in the month of August 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you draft the statement, did you type it up, or was it Mr. Dragan Tasic who typed it up on his computer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: No, I drafted the statement, and my son typed it up on a computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's your son who typed it up on the computer. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I certified that statement at court, and I handed it over to Mr. Seselj's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions of a technical nature to put to you. You have explained to us how things took place with the OTP and with Mr. Seselj's Defence team. Now, this is my first question of a technical nature, which is a fairly straightforward question which I'm sure you'll be able to answer. I read, in the judgement concerning Colonel Mrkic and Captain Sljivancanin, that the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party were part of a unit called the White Eagles. I was a little bit surprised on reading this, and I checked to see whether there was a footnote. There is no footnote. I therefore wonder where this comes from, i.e., the fact that the volunteers were called White Eagles. Since you met volunteers, since you were, yourself, as it appears, a volunteer, can you explain to us whether the White Eagles were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely incorrect. The volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Vukovar belonged to a unit called Leva Supoderica, which belonged to the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. And, as such, it was under the operative command of the Guards Brigade under the command of Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is now my second question of a technical nature. I have very few questions for you. My colleagues will put the bulk of the question to you. I have noted, in the statement you challenge, which you gave to the OTP on the 19th of September, 2006, in paragraph 54 - you don't have the statement before you, but you don't need to look at it - at some point you talk about the Milosevic regime, and you say that the Milosevic regime was against the Chetniks. You say that Milosevic's regime was in favour of Communism, that it was competing with nationalist parties like the Serbian Radical Party, and you say that the co-operation between the Milosevic regime and Mr. Seselj deteriorated because of the JNA. Did you tell this to the OTP? Is this right, is this not right? What can you say about that today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I said something to that effect. It is true that Milosevic's regime, in principle, was against the Chetnik movement. Mr. Milosevic's party was the Socialist Party of Serbia, which originated directly from the League of Communists of Serbia. As everybody knows, Communists and Serbian Chetniks were never in an amicable relation. I apologise. Do you have any other questions? Actually, your question was long and I don't remember all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in is this: I'm putting the question to you for the following reason. According to the Prosecutor, Mr. Seselj is a member of a joint criminal enterprise, together with Mr. Milosevic, together with Mr. Karadzic, who is being tried by this Tribunal, together with Simatovic and a number of others. As it seems you were familiar with the way the Serbian Radical Party operated, you were partly aware of this, I would like you to give us your opinion on the relations between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic and his regime, if there was such a thing as Milosevic's regime. What were the relations between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Seselj were political opponents at first. On the most important points, such as why we sent off volunteers, I believe that's the most important thing to explain. We, as a nationalist party, felt it was our obligation to protect the Serbian population outside the territories of the then Republic of Serbia. There was no open co-operation with the regime of Slobodan Milosevic, but it would have been illogical to expect that in the middle of a war there would be an armed conflict between the Serb Radical Party and the then Socialist Party of Serbia, led by the president, Slobodan Milosevic. The Serbian Radical Party had its own priorities; first and foremost among them, to protect the Serbian population outside Serbia. Later on, in peacetime, of course, we would have fought for power, and in that struggle we would be against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. I read about your political career, which you described to the OTP, with great interest. You were pressured; maybe you were, maybe you weren't. From what I understood, and if I make a mistake, please let me know, but you, yourself, were an anti-Communist, and in Germany in 1987 in Offenbach, you joined the Ravna Gora organisation, and after that, when you were in Serbia, the joined the SAVA association, and it is only after that time that you joined the Serbian Radical Party. What I would like you to confirm is this: Before belonging to the Serbian Radical Party, was your political path totally different from that of Mr. Seselj's?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I would like to make one correction. I was not a member of the Serb Radical Party. I was a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and I was involved in the creation of the Serbian Chetnik Movement together with Mr. Seselj. In fact, I was one of the first founders of that movement. The Serbian Chetnik Movement was later merged with another party to create the Serb Radical Party, but that was towards the end of February 1991. All the rest that you said is correct. I was part of the Chetnik emigration movement. I was a member of Ravna Gora in Offenbach. Then after returning to Serbia, I was in prison for a while in a prison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake, perhaps, in your statement of the 19th of January, 2004. In paragraph 11, you listed the Serbian Radical Party: President Mr. Seselj, Deputy President Djordjevic, Petkovic, Stefanovic, Goskovic [phoen], Viletic [phoen]. And then list of members: Zoran Drizilovic [phoen], aka Zika, and after that there is your name, Zoran Rankic, and after that there is Jovan --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction. Mr. President, it is clearly stated in paragraph 11 that it was the Serbian Chetnik Movement, not the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is, therefore, a list that concerns the Serbian Chetnik Movement, which means that you have never been a member of the Serbian Radical Party; in other words, you have never had your membership card of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... officially a member of the Serbian Radical Party, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you have never been a member of the Serbian Radical Party, how is it, then, that according to the statements you gave to the OTP, that you were present in the offices of the War Staff, headed by Petkovic? How was it that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I would have to explain that. Towards the end of February 1991, the Serbian Chetnik Movement merged with a spin-off wing of the Serbian Radical Party, and there was a conference in Kragujevac, if I remember correctly, where the Serbian Radical Party was established. A central homeland administration was created, and members of this popular radical party that merged with the Serbian Chetnik Movement were in that central homeland administration. They were represented proportionally, and I was part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand things better now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be of assistance with my remarks. When the creation --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the creation --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj should use his time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, yes, of course. But Mr. Seselj is trying to help the Judges, and when someone is trying to help me, I never turn down any help. But maybe you can also help me, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and I'd be happy to help the Court. But what Mr. Seselj is doing is testifying, in terms of what he thinks the reality is, and he's giving you his representation about the issue that the Court has asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if we do not consider what Mr. Seselj has said, if at no point in time you were a member of the Serbian Radical Party, nonetheless, you are telling us that you were affiliated to the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and this is why, at some point in time, you were part of a much broader movement at the same time as Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to explain. I did not need to get a new membership card, because two parties merged, the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Popular Radical Party, and the Serb Radical Party was formed with that name. However, the membership cards remained bearing the name of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. I did not need to have my membership card replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already spent enough time on my questions, and I shall give the floor to my colleagues, who have a lot of questions for you. I don't know who will start. Courtesy would have it that it is Ms. Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it will be Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, in extension of what the Presiding Judge has already told you, I think it would be pertinent to just add a few extra details. First of all, Mr. Rankic, you have been called here to testify today and tomorrow by the Chamber. This means that you are not a witness of the Prosecution, nor are you a witness for the accused. We have called you as our witness because we wanted to avoid any possible misunderstanding as to whose interests you may have thought that you were here to defend. You are here, sir, to tell the truth, and you have made the solemn declaration. And I wish to remind you that there is a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete evidence to this Tribunal. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Secondly, I would like to just inform you that for technical reasons, we have to have a break every 90 minutes because the tapes from the recordings of these proceedings have to be changed. And if you look at the clock, you'll see that this is in four and a half minutes. So this means that we will take a 20-minute break in four and a half minutes, and then we will resume and go on for another 90 minutes, and then have another break, and then we will adjourn at 7.00. That will be it for today, and then we will proceed tomorrow, as the Presiding Judge has instructed you. Mr. President, I don't know if it would make sense, actually, to take the break now and then I will proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the break now. Witness, I was told that you sometimes suffered from backache. If it is too trying for you, please let us know so that you can have a rest and relax, if you need to. Make the most of the 20-minute break. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rankic, before we begin my examination, I would like to clarify one further thing with you, and that is the fact that you are not under suspicion. You are not being accused. There are no allegations to be made towards you. You are here only as a witness, and nothing that you are saying today in your testimony here in this court can be used by this Court against you, unless, of course, you testify falsely or incompletely. So I just want to make sure that you are not the accused here, you are a witness, and you're supposed to tell the truth. Now, Mr. Rankic, what I want to elicit from you is your account of the process of recruiting volunteers through the SRS in 1991 and 1992. You were a member of the leadership of the party of the SCP, of the Chetnik Movement, and you were close to the proceedings and the procedures that applied to the process of recruiting volunteers, so I'd like you to account to us, as briefly as you can, the process of how a young man in, say, Bosnia, or even in Serbia, could become an SRS volunteer. What -- how does the career as an SRS volunteer begin? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I have to clear up one thing. I'm qualified to speak about events until the end of 1991, the moment when I resigned to the post of deputy chief of the working headquarters of the SRS -- or, rather, the Serbian Chetnik Movement. From that time on, I had no obligations towards the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party, but I can explain what happened in the course of 1991. The establishment of the Crisis Staff in the spring of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Rankic. I'm perfectly aware of the time in which you were a member of the party, but I believe that you are still able to provide us with your evidence even in 1992. So my questions to you are not limited to what you experienced as a member of the leadership of the SRS or SCP party. It's your personal account that I am interested in. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I agree, but this version for 1991 is an official version. After that time, it's my individual version. Beginning with the establishment of the Crisis Staff in the spring of 1991 and the arrival of large numbers of refugees from the territory of Croatia, the first tasks of the Crisis Staff were to find accommodation for the refugees and to assist -- when I say "assist," I don't mean financial assistance, because we couldn't afford that, but aid in food, medicines, et cetera. After sporadic incidents in the territory of Croatia, the armed conflict expanded, and the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Radical Party started receiving requests from crisis staffs in Croatia to give them help in manpower. At our sessions of the Crisis Staff, we decided it would be possible and feasible to send volunteers to Croatia, of course, once we were satisfied that these volunteers were absolutely indispensable there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Why would crisis staffs in Croatia call the SRS Crisis Staff in Belgrade for manpower? Did you advertise the ability to organise the sending of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what it was. In actual fact, in the beginning of 1991 the only legal army at the time, the JNA, took a neutral position. They were more a buffer between enemy forces than fighting on any side in areas, of course, where the JNA was present. Where the JNA was not present, the conflict was open. We had declared ourselves as a nationalist party. There were other parties in Serbia, of course, but not with the same orientation. It was quite logical for them to address themselves to us as a nationalist party, because that was our standing. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me one thing. The crisis staffs that asked you for assistance, whose crisis staffs were they? Were they the municipal crisis staffs in the various municipalities in Croatia or were they the SRS crisis staffs? In which organisational context did these crisis staffs operate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: It was the crisis staffs of the Territorial Defence in areas of what was then the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: So we would receive fax messages in the office of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Radical Party. And considering that we had an intensive co-operation with the Association of Serbs in Croatia, then headed by the retired general, Mr. Pekic, we wanted to know his opinion as well, because he was more familiar with the situation in Croatia than us. If he told us that in a given area there was real need for manpower, then we would convene the municipal boards of the Serbian Radical Party or the Serbian Chetnik Movement - these didn't matter anymore because we acted in a united way - and ask them to make lists of volunteers who were prepared to go to Croatia, to areas where the Serb population was in danger, to defend them. The JNA at the time was not very active, and the response to JNA mobilisation call-ups was very poor because certain parties, which were not of nationalist orientation, but of a different orientation, and we personally saw them as traitor parties, worked to reduce the response to JNA mobilisation call-ups. If you need a more extensive explanation, I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We may get back to this. But can I just ask you about this retired general, Mr. Pekic. Was he considered to be a nationalist also?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, although he used to be a Communist general, but probably later, when these things started happening in Croatia, he changed his views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So while the JNA was unable or unwilling to provide any real assistance to the Serbian nationalist side, we had this retired general who was on the scene in Croatia and was able to determine the areas where manpower assistance was needed. Was it then him who facilitated, through the crisis staffs of the TOs in Croatia, the requests that were made to the party in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the president of the Association of Serbs in Croatia and outside Croatia, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So then you took contact with the TOs, if I understood you correctly, and made an assessment of how many men were needed to go to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then, if I understood you correctly, you mobilised these men through the local branches of the SRS party in Croatia, where such branches existed. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: No, not in Croatia. In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks for this clarification. So through the SRS branches in Serbia, you got in contact with young men who were willing to go to Croatia to fight on the Serbian side. That's very well. Now, these --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: These young men, where did they report to? Did they go to their local branch or did they have to show up in Belgrade, at your office, for the purpose of recruitment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: They would report to the local headquarters or branches of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party. These branches would make a list, and then they would come to Belgrade, where the central headquarters were, where the Crisis Staff was. And then they would be escorted and transported to areas where they were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll get to that in just a minute. My question is: Apart from the young men who reported directly to the SRS branches in the various municipalities, did young men also spontaneously address themselves to the municipal authorities, to the TOs, or to the crisis staffs in Serbia in order to sign up as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't really understand that question. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would, and forgive me for perhaps putting the question a bit unclear to you. I'm asking because I read somewhere, in some of your statements, that young men were also referred to the SRS party in Belgrade by the municipal authorities, meaning that it wasn't only through the SRS branches that the young men were guided to go to your office in Belgrade, it was also through the municipal authorities, the TOs and perhaps the crisis staffs. So I just wanted to clarify if the municipal authorities would also and could also advise young men to report to the SRS main office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: That must be a mistake. I was talking about the municipal boards of the Serbian Radical Party. Everyone else who wanted to sign up went through military authorities. There was a military department in every municipality, and everyone could sign up into the JNA through those military departments. I hope you understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I do, and I was obviously mistaken. So it was exclusively through the SRS's own party machinery that the recruitments took place? The municipal authorities did not assist in this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Every municipality, as I said, had a military department for those who wanted to sign up into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. At one point, the young men started showing up in Belgrade, and they wanted to volunteer. What did you do with them at that point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: From that moment on, a central list had to be made, and they all had to have their military service books on them, because one of the conditions to go into the field was to have completed compulsory military service. We tried to make sure not to send alcoholics or criminals. Of course, if we were able to check their files, but our ability to do that was limited. If somebody had a mental health problem, that would normally be written in their military service book. Then we would bus them to a destination. And once there, we would turn them over to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, on whose orders they were sent, and then the TO would take charge of their accommodation, food for them, and providing weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. So first there was a screening of the volunteers, where you looked through their military booklets and where you were able to take out those who had indications of alcoholism or other mental reasons. Did you train them, and how was that organised, and where did you train them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, in the early days before we started joining directly the JNA, we had a centre for training volunteers in Prigrevica. I don't know if it can really be called a training centre because it was a very accelerated course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How long did it last, and who were the teachers, and what was the curriculum during this training? What did they learn?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: That centre was set up with the assistance of General Pekic. He had brought two instructors who said they had been members of the elite 63rd Parachute Brigade. The courses were short, around 15 days. During the course, the men would be acquainted with certain types of weapons, certain types of combat, and a combination of tactical and fitness training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The instructors that General Pekic used, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as members of the 63rd Parachute Brigade, which is an elite unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did General Pekic, himself, take part in the training?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: No, he did not, but he did send them. At least that's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how many volunteers were trained at the same time, roughly, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: They were in groups of 20, 30, 40 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So groups of 20 to 40 young men were sent on a two weeks' training course with two professional soldiers from the elite unit that you mentioned. After that -- that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so after that, they were ready for deployment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, how was the process in deciding which places they would be sent to, and how many would go to each place? How was that decision made? Was that exclusively made in the Crisis Staff of the SRS party, where you sat, or did you involve Pekic or others in the decision, or eventually were the -- the local TOs in Croatia, were they also heard on the matter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the local Territorial Defence requests in Croatia, we sent a certain number of volunteers to each of those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who decided the number of volunteers to be sent to each place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: It was part of their request. They specified how many volunteers, approximately, they would need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the decision to select each individual volunteer to go to this place or to that place, that was the decision that was taken in the SRS War Staff, is that correct, that is to say, by you and your fellow members?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: It depended on priorities. The priority was the kind of situation where volunteers were sent. If the crisis had escalated, where there were hotbeds of crisis, we considered those places a priority, and that's where we sent more volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that. I just want to make sure that I understand fully that the selection of each individual volunteer was your selection. Nobody else was involved in that? I'm talking about the Crisis Staff of the SRS party at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, so now we have selected some young volunteers that are going to one place and another number of young volunteers are going to another place in Croatia in 1991. Then you told me that they were transported by bus up to the various places, and there they were handed over to the TOs. How did the transportation take place, how was that done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Buses would come to Prigrevica. That's where the volunteers got on the buses. They would go to Croatia, accompanied by lists. They would be handed over to the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence members would sign the list confirming their receipt. They would keep a copy of the signed list, and one was sent back to me, and I would then hand it over to the staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Whose buses were they? Who paid for the buses or who organised the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: The buses were organised by the Association of Serbs who had been residents of Croatia but now resided in Serbia, and that was at the beginning. And later on, it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you say that at some point the buses were organised by the JNA to transport the SRS volunteers to the field; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct, after the 1st October 1991, and after the immediate threat of war was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I just want to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- one little detail. I read somewhere in your statement, and to be honest, I can't remember where, that Mr. Petkovic was in close contact with, I think, the Ministry for Relations with Serbians Outside Serbia or something, in organising this transport. Can you confirm this, or was that misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: There is an error there, or perhaps somebody did not interpret my words properly on purpose. Mr. Petkovic and myself on one occasion went to the Ministry for Relations with Serbians Outside Serbia, which was the ministry of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, and Minister Petkovic said that he was supposed to have a private conversation with Mr. Cvijan. I was with him in the ministry, but I was sitting in front of the office while they were in the office talking for some 10 minutes. I don't know what they were talking about. He told me that the conversation would be private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure. I'm not in any way interested in breaking into the confidentiality. My only interest was to find out whether in any way the ministry was providing assistance to the transportation of volunteers to the combat zones.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then you arrive to the local TO where you were supposed to hand over the detainees. Did you travel with the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The interpreter interpreted the word "detainees." I suppose you referred to volunteers, whereas the interpreter interpreted your words as if you had said "detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. No, I think -- I think, actually, it was my mistake. I meant to say "the volunteers."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Mr. Harhoff. I'm looking at the transcript in English, and your words were correct. You said "volunteers," and the interpreter says "detainees" on purpose. You have to intervene immediately. You have to replace the interpreters. This is not the first time that they are misinterpreting on purpose. You've been saying "volunteers" all the time. Why would they interpret your words as if you had said "detainees"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have full confidence in the interpreters, and I'm sure that there's no intention to change the substance of what I'm saying. I thought -- it struck me that I thought I was the one who actually used the word "detainees," and I realised, as soon as I said it, that it was wrong. I meant to say "volunteers," of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you did, Your Honour. At page 45, line 21, the transcript actually says "hand over the detainees" in your question, so the accused is not correctly representing what is in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In any case, let's move on. This is not material. My question to you, Mr. Rankic, was whether you escorted your volunteers to the takers, so to say, the institutions who would receive them, and I can't remember your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I said that in most cases, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was, then, the procedure when you stood face to face with the local TO commander, with 20 volunteers behind you? How did the exchange proceed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I handed over the list with volunteers, and then he would sign confirming that they had arrived. There were two copies of that list. He would keep one copy for himself, and the other copy I returned to the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Radical Party. In the meantime, while I was there, they were duty-bound to show me that those volunteers would be billeted, that they would receive weapons and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the volunteers came in their civilian clothes to the TO in Croatia, and there they were given uniforms and weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What sort of uniforms were they given; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: At first, those were classical olive-drab JNA uniforms, and later on there were also camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: It was a standard-issue type of weapons that existed in the JNA, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: M-48 to M-56 rifles. There were also M-57s and automatic rifles, M-70. But that was all later. At first, we would be issued with obsolete weapons, such as Thompson and Spagins, those kind of weapons that the JNA had written off and kept in reserve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The weapons which the volunteers were given, were they the same as -- the same kind of weapons as the weapons used in the two weeks' training prior to the deployment? In other words, were the volunteers familiar with the weapons that they were issued by the TOs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So you gave him the lists of, assuming it was a man, of the volunteers, and you handed over the volunteers to the TO, and the TO would then provide them with uniforms and weapons and accommodation. Did you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: And food, yes, as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Did you ever receive any confirmation that now the TO had taken over the command of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: At the moment they stamped the list, they confirmed that they had taken over the volunteers. The list was stamped, and it was signed by the commander of the TO, and that was my confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you then brought the stamped and signed list back to the head office in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were the volunteers paid for their service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at first not a single volunteer received any money for anything. Later on, when we fell under the JNA, they enjoyed some privileges, like any other mobilised recruit, anybody who was forcibly mobilised. Before the 1st of October, 1991, nobody received anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the volunteers had to sign a receipt for the weapons that they were given at the TOs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know. And people showed me some papers, some documents proving that they had been issued with weapons, and I'm saying that in respect of the volunteers who had come back from their field missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that leads me to the next question; namely, were the volunteers asked to give back the weapon before they left the place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Between Serbia and Croatia, there was border -- state border police, and nobody could cross the border to Serbia carrying a long-barrelled rifle, unless, of course, they smuggled them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did that happen; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, it probably happened. I suppose it did. I don't know, but I am inclined to think that it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Other than the volunteers who were either killed or wounded, did any of them remain in the areas of combat after they had completed their first task or did they all return to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: You said "detainees," or I'm receiving a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I guess I may have made the same mistake again. I apologise for this. We've been sitting in another trial this morning, where all the talk was about detainees, so maybe this word is just circling in my head. But I meant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please let me finish. I meant to say "volunteers," of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. Harhoff. Again, I'm looking at the English transcript, and I don't see the word "detainees" anywhere. I'm inviting Mr. Marcussen to find it. A little while ago, he pretended that he had found it, when it was already long gone from the screen. There is no word "detainees" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Drop it. You can take it up later on. Let me proceed with my examination. My question to you, Mr. Rankic, was whether all the volunteers returned to Centar, so to say, or whether some of them stayed and continued on their own.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: It all depended on the needs on the ground. Some volunteers joined the police force on the ground and some returned. It all depended on the situation as it was in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you maintain any sort of contact with your volunteers while they were in combat under the command of the TO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I even went there to visit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those visits?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: To inspect their conditions of life, to see what the discipline was, and if there were any problems that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was it necessary to nurse them? I mean, you had signed off command over them to the TO, and I suppose that they were involved in the armed forces under the TO's command. So if there were any problems, the TO would report to you; otherwise, it would be unnecessary to go and inspect on your own?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, if -- even if I hadn't been the deputy chief of the War Staff, I would have done it as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if other volunteer units also came to the conflict areas in Croatia, that is to say, volunteers who had not been sent by the SRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who sent those other volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the case of Arkan's volunteers or the Serbian Volunteer Guard. I'm also familiar with the case of Mirko Jovic or the White Eagles. Anybody else could go on their own, as a private individual, without the backing of any organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if these volunteers were recruited according to the same procedure as the SRS volunteers were recruited; that is to say, if they were recruited on the basis of demands made by the TOs or requests made by the TOs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how they went. I'm not familiar with the procedure at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you know if the requests that you received from the TOs were also sent to others?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When you described to me that the TOs were sending out requests for assistance in the form of young combatants, and you also told me that Arkan's men were represented, the White Eagles were represented, and other volunteer groups were present in the area, it would suggest to me, at least, that there was a market out there for volunteers. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to word all that. I worked with the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just ask one more question in relation to the contact that you held with the volunteers while they were in service. How long did you retain your contact with the SRS volunteers; for a couple of months, or until the end of the war, or how long?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's when you resigned, but do you know if the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the Crisis Staff of the SRS continued their contacts with the volunteers after you resigned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the contacts went on, but I'm not familiar with the details thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: At several places in your statements, Mr. Rankic, you mentioned Milan Lancuzanin, and you said that he was the Chetnik commander in Vukovar, and that some of the SRS volunteers were put under his command. What was Lancuzanin's position? Was he an officer in the JNA, or did he work for the TO, or where was he placed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Lancuzanin was the commander of the Leva Supoderica Unit on the strength of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. He was not an active JNA officer. And you just said he was a Chetnik commander. I don't agree with that expression, because all of us were Chetniks in their eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue boils down to under whose command he was. Was he under the TO's command or under the JNA's command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: Under the command of the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence was under the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Under the Guards Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade did have operative command in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the JNA Guards Brigade have the overall authority to direct the units in the area during the combat operations? In other words, Mr. Rankic, I'm looking for who was holding the overall military command in Vukovar, just to take one example, during the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC
utterances.text: I must put it this way: The city of Vukovar, itself, was divided into two sectors, Sector North and Sector South. As far as I know, the operative command was in the hands of the Novi Sad Corps in Sector North. I believe that the commander was General Bjorcevic [phoen]. And in OZ South, the operative command was in the hands of the Guards Brigade of the JNA, under the command of General Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
